title: Measuring Metabolism From the Outside
endLine: At steady state, oxygen used and heat lost reveal metabolic rate.

scenes.tts: How do you measure metabolism inside a body without opening it? Every living system trades oxygen, carbon dioxide, and heat with its surroundings. Seal it in a chamber, and those flows expose the hidden engine.
scenes.caption: How do you measure metabolism inside a body without opening it? Every living system trades oxygen, carbon dioxide, and heat with its surroundings. Seal it in a chamber, and those flows expose the hidden engine.
scenes.visual: A large sealed transparent chamber fills two-thirds of the frame height, holding a schematic resting mammal with a glowing question mark at its core. Slow drifting particles move in as oxygen and out as carbon dioxide while soft heat ripples radiate outward toward the chamber walls. On 'those flows expose the hidden engine', two live gauges illuminate on the chamber's right wall: an oxygen trace and a heat-flow meter, both labelled schematic.
scenes.narration: How do you measure metabolism inside a body without opening it? Every living system trades oxygen, carbon dioxide, and heat with its surroundings. Seal it in a chamber, and those flows expose the hidden engine.

scenes.visual: The sealed chamber dims gently while gas particles keep drifting; high-contrast title text appears at center: 'Measuring Metabolism From the Outside'.

scenes.tts: Start with oxygen, a method called respirometry. Compare air entering a lung with air leaving. Air enters at about twenty-one percent oxygen and leaves at about sixteen percent. Twenty-one minus sixteen leaves about five percent of its volume taken up as oxygen. Multiply that drop by the air breathed to get oxygen use.
scenes.caption: Start with oxygen, a method called respirometry. Compare air entering a lung with air leaving. Air enters at about 21% oxygen and leaves at about 16%. 21 minus 16 leaves about 5% of its volume taken up as oxygen. Multiply that drop by the air breathed to get oxygen use.
scenes.visual: On the same sealed chamber, an inlet duct highlights an incoming air bar at 21% O₂ and an outlet duct shows 16% O₂ leaving the schematic lung. As each number is spoken, the subtraction '21% − 16% = 5%' builds step by step beside the chamber (computed from these values). On 'multiply', a '× air breathed' term joins it and the live oxygen-uptake trace begins to climb (trace labelled 'schematic').
scenes.narration: Start with oxygen, a method called respirometry. Compare air entering a lung with air leaving. Air enters at about 21% oxygen and leaves at about 16%. 21 minus 16 leaves about 5% of its volume taken up as oxygen. Multiply that drop by the air breathed to get oxygen use.

scenes.tts: Now follow heat: calorimetry. Metabolic rate is energy used per unit time, in watts, and nearly all becomes heat. At steady state, body temperature holds constant, so no heat is stored. Heat made plus heat gained equals dry leak plus evaporation. Dry leak means radiation, contact and moving air.
scenes.caption: Now follow heat: calorimetry. Metabolic rate is energy used per unit time, in watts, and nearly all becomes heat. At steady state, body temperature holds constant, so no heat is stored. Heat made plus heat gained equals dry leak plus evaporation. Dry leak means radiation, contact and moving air.
scenes.visual: The chamber's heat-flow gauge brightens while a thermometer on the schematic animal holds flat at a steady mark. A balance equation builds in sync with speech: 'M + G = C × (Tb − Ta) + E', with plain-word labels beneath (heat made, heat gained, dry leak, evaporation; schematic). On 'dry leak', three small arrows leave the animal's skin: 'radiation', 'contact', 'moving air'.
scenes.narration: Now follow heat: calorimetry. Metabolic rate is energy used per unit time, in watts, and nearly all becomes heat. At steady state, body temperature holds constant, so no heat is stored. Heat made plus heat gained equals dry leak plus evaporation. Dry leak means radiation, contact and moving air.

scenes.tts: With nothing heating the animal, heat made equals heat lost. Burning fuel also uses oxygen roughly in step with the energy released. So at steady state, oxygen used and heat lost reveal metabolic rate.
scenes.visual: Same chamber and equation. The 'G' term dims to '0', leaving 'M = heat lost' highlighted. Then the oxygen trace and the heat-loss readout light up together on the chamber wall, joined by a bracket labelled 'metabolic rate' (schematic).
scenes.caption: With nothing heating the animal, heat made equals heat lost. Burning fuel also uses oxygen roughly in step with the energy released. So at steady state, oxygen used and heat lost reveal metabolic rate.

scenes.tts: Carbon dioxide adds a second clue, but one pathway tests it. In the pentose phosphate pathway, one step releases carbon dioxide without using any oxygen. Predict: does running that pathway raise the whole body's carbon dioxide to oxygen ratio?
scenes.caption: Carbon dioxide adds a second clue, but one pathway tests it. In the pentose phosphate pathway, one step releases carbon dioxide without using any oxygen. Predict: does running that pathway raise the whole body's CO₂/O₂ ratio?
scenes.visual: Beside the same chamber, a live CO₂/O₂ ratio dial appears next to the oxygen trace (schematic). Inside the schematic body, a glowing side branch releases one CO₂ bubble with zero O₂ entering it. The ratio needle freezes beside a question mark, and high-contrast question text appears above the chamber: 'Does this raise the body's CO₂/O₂ ratio?'
scenes.narration: Carbon dioxide adds a second clue, but one pathway tests it. In the pentose phosphate pathway, one step releases carbon dioxide without using any oxygen. Predict: does running that pathway raise the whole body's CO₂/O₂ ratio?

scenes.visual: The question remains on screen for 4.5 seconds while the CO₂/O₂ dial needle gently wobbles near its starting mark with a subtle ambient pulse.

scenes.tts: Surprisingly, no. That step also makes N A D P H, an electron carrier. Cells later spend it on oxygen-using reactions or on making fat. So the pathway alone does not raise the body's carbon dioxide to oxygen ratio. To measure that pathway, experimenters use tracers that follow glucose's first carbon, the one this step releases.
scenes.caption: Surprisingly, no. That step also makes NADPH, an electron carrier. Cells later spend it on oxygen-using reactions or on making fat. So the pathway alone does not raise the body's CO₂/O₂ ratio. To measure that pathway, experimenters use tracers that follow glucose's first carbon, the one this step releases.
scenes.visual: The CO₂/O₂ dial settles flat on baseline (schematic). From the highlighted side branch, an NADPH arrow flows onward into oxygen-using reactions and fat synthesis, keeping the ratio level. A bright marker labelled 'C1 tracer' tags a schematic glucose dot to show how pathway flux is measured instead.
scenes.narration: Surprisingly, no. That step also makes NADPH, an electron carrier. Cells later spend it on oxygen-using reactions or on making fat. So the pathway alone does not raise the body's CO₂/O₂ ratio. To measure that pathway, experimenters use tracers that follow glucose's first carbon, the one this step releases.

scenes.tts: Chambers need controls. First, wait for steady state, when flows and body temperature hold constant and no heat is stored. Second, hold air and walls at the same temperature, so dry heat leaks toward one known temperature.
scenes.caption: Chambers need controls. First, wait for steady state, when flows and body temperature hold constant and no heat is stored. Second, hold air and walls at the same temperature, so dry heat leaks toward one known temperature.
scenes.visual: Two control checks animate on the same chamber (all schematic). First, a drifting temperature trace levels flat and turns steady. Second, a warmer chamber wall cools to match the chamber air temperature so one thermometer reading 'Ta' governs both, and the dry-leak arrows point toward that single value.
scenes.narration: Chambers need controls. First, wait for steady state, when flows and body temperature hold constant and no heat is stored. Second, hold air and walls at the same temperature, so dry heat leaks toward one known temperature.

scenes.tts: Oxygen records unlocked landmarks. Szent-Györgyi and then Krebs measured oxygen use in minced pigeon breast muscle. A pinch of four-carbon acid made the muscle burn far more oxygen than oxidizing it could explain. The acid was not spent as fuel; it was reused to burn other fuel, revealing the citric acid cycle.
scenes.caption: Oxygen records unlocked landmarks. Szent-Györgyi and then Krebs measured oxygen use in minced pigeon breast muscle. A pinch of four-carbon acid made the muscle burn far more oxygen than oxidizing it could explain. The acid was not spent as fuel; it was reused to burn other fuel, revealing the citric acid cycle.
scenes.visual: The same sealed chamber scales down smoothly to hold schematic flecks of minced pigeon breast muscle wired to the live oxygen trace on the right. A tiny pinch drops in; the oxygen trace plunges far deeper than a small fuel-sized bar could explain, while a glowing circular arrow loops inside the chamber to show reuse (schematic). Label: 'Szent-Györgyi & Krebs'.
scenes.narration: Oxygen records unlocked landmarks. Szent-Györgyi and then Krebs measured oxygen use in minced pigeon breast muscle. A pinch of four-carbon acid made the muscle burn far more oxygen than oxidizing it could explain. The acid was not spent as fuel; it was reused to burn other fuel, revealing the citric acid cycle.

scenes.tts: An oxygen electrode tracks the oxygen left around isolated mitochondria. Adding A D P, spent A T P, steepened the slow oxygen line: State three. Once the A D P became A T P, it flattened: State four. The respiratory chain burns the oxygen but never touches A D P; A T P synthase does.
scenes.caption: An oxygen electrode tracks the oxygen left around isolated mitochondria. Adding ADP, spent ATP, steepened the slow oxygen line: State 3. Once the ADP became ATP, it flattened: State 4. The respiratory chain burns the oxygen but never touches ADP; ATP synthase does.
scenes.visual: Inside the same small chamber, an oxygen electrode probe dips into schematic isolated mitochondria. The live oxygen trace on the right slopes down slowly, bends steeply downward on a drop labelled 'ADP' (tagged 'State 3'), then flattens again when ATP accumulates (tagged 'State 4'; schematic). Two separate schematic icons appear: 'respiratory chain' consuming O₂ and 'ATP synthase' taking in ADP, with no line between them yet.
scenes.narration: An oxygen electrode tracks the oxygen left around isolated mitochondria. Adding ADP, spent ATP, steepened the slow oxygen line: State 3. Once the ADP became ATP, it flattened: State 4. The respiratory chain burns the oxygen but never touches ADP; ATP synthase does.

scenes.tts: In 1961, Peter Mitchell proposed that a proton gradient links the two. From whole mammals to isolated mitochondria, measure what crosses a controlled boundary, and hidden metabolism comes into view.
scenes.caption: In 1961, Peter Mitchell proposed that a proton gradient links the two. From whole mammals to isolated mitochondria, measure what crosses a controlled boundary, and hidden metabolism comes into view.
scenes.visual: First, the two icons from the last scene are linked across a sealed membrane by glowing proton arrows labelled 'Mitchell 1961 (proposed)'. Then the chamber zooms smoothly back out from mitochondria to the whole schematic resting mammal; both live gauges, oxygen use and heat balance, glow steadily together as the core question mark fades into a clear active meter.
scenes.narration: In 1961, Peter Mitchell proposed that a proton gradient links the two. From whole mammals to isolated mitochondria, measure what crosses a controlled boundary, and hidden metabolism comes into view.

scenes.visual: Clean dark end card showing the take-home line verbatim in large high-contrast type: 'At steady state, oxygen used and heat lost reveal metabolic rate.'
